doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Armstrong, Bunny Berigan and the Saturday Night Swing Session
summary: What Armstrong meant to him, and Bunny Berigan as the next big influence on radio.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Okay, so Louis Armstrong enters your life.
Were you curious as to what is it he’s doing?
What is it that he is doing? Is he reading this music?
Yeah. I mean how did your thought process go to try to figure out what it was?

You know I really didn’t try to intellectualize it at all, I just knew I heard that sound and it carried so much emotion and expression and everything that it just flipped me out. And then the next big guy was this guy Bunny Berigan. He was actually, you know Louis once said, when asked who his favorite trumpet player was, “My boy is Bunny.” And I know why, because Bunny was actually an outgrowth of Louis. Bunny used to say when you go on the road all you need is a toothbrush and some Louis records. Bunny was doing studio work in New York, long before I ever came near New York City of course. And he had a program called “The Saturday Night Swing Session.” Leith Stevens was the CBS conductor. And they featured Bunny. And he opened. And this was long before he recorded “I Can’t Get Started,” which was in 1936, he opened that show with the pick- ups [sings] I’ve flown around the world— and so forth. And I heard that and that was another thing. I’d like to talk, I know there is time on the session, but briefly about a friend from the hills there, he lived in Springville, New York, his name is Bill Simon. He lives in Florida.
